card: Russian marks register strongly. **ты** and **вы** are only the start: vocabulary (**приобрести́** or **купи́ть**), sentence length, names (**Ива́н Петро́вич** or **Ва́ня**) and particles all change between official, neutral and colloquial speech. Mixing them is the most noticeable C1 slip.

sections.body: Native speakers notice register before grammar. An email to a professor that opens **Приве́т!** and a chat with friends in office Russian both sound wrong.

sections.title: Names and address
sections.body: Officially: first name + patronymic and **вы**: **Ива́н Петро́вич, вы не могли́ бы…?** Among friends: a short name and **ты**: **Ва́ня, мо́жешь…?** Switching to **ты** is an event, and the older or more senior person usually offers: **Дава́йте перейдём на ты.**

sections.title: Colloquial features
sections.body: Everyday speech drops words and adds particles: **Ты куда́?** (no verb), **Ну, дава́й!**, **Ла́дно.**, **Я же говори́л!**, **Вот и всё.** Keep these out of formal writing.

sections.title: Officialese
sections.body: Official style piles up nouns: **осуществле́ние контро́ля за выполне́нием**. Good writers avoid it; in your own writing, prefer a verb: **контроли́ровать**.

mistakes.why: A name and patronymic go with **здра́вствуйте** and **вы**.

examples.ru: Здра́вствуйте, Ива́н Петро́вич! Вы не могли́ бы мне помо́чь?
examples.en: Hello, Ivan Petrovich! Could you help me?
Vanya, give me a hand, will you?
